*143. SHRIMATI BRINDA KARAT: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) what is Government's policy regarding clinical trials being conducted 
by multinational companies in the country; 
(b) the steps taken by Government for regulating such clinical trials; 
(c) whether Government have any mechanism to monitor/regulate such 
medical trials; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; and 
(e) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. 
ANBUMANI RAMADOSS) :(a) to (e) Re gulations for conducting clinical 
trial in the country including by multinational companies are prescribed 
under Rule-122 DA-122-E and Schedule-Y to the Rules. The Rules provide 
specific application from and relevant document requirements for seeking 
permission 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
8 

[2 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
to conduct clinical trials. The data/d ocuments are evaluated in consultation 
with subject experts. 
Permission to conduct phase-l trial, including first time use in human 
beings, is presently not granted for new drugs developed outside the country. 
For drugs developed outside the country — multicentric clinical trials at 
phase-ll and III stage are permitted after similar trial protocol has been 
approved by regulatory authorities of the countries where such drugs have 
been invented. Permission to conduct trials on new drugs invented outside 
the country takes into consideration the permissions granted by stringent 
ICH countries (viz. USA, EU, Japan, etc.) 
Schedule-Y, which prescribes requirements for permission to conduct 
clinical trials was introduced in 1988. The amended version, notified in 
February, 2005, after extensive revision, lays down stringent and specific 
procedures that need to be followed by Sponsors, Investigators as well as 
Ethics committees. The amendmen t lays special emphasis on the 
modalities for obtaining informed consent from clinical trial subjects, and 
the language to be used for consent fo rms have also been prescribed. The 
Rules also require that prior approval of Institutional Ethics Committee 
has to be obtained before undertaking any clinical trial in the country. 
Membership criteria as well as conduct of Ethics Committee meetings 
have also been prescribed in the amendment. The revision has been made 
in consultation with experts including experts from ICMR, with the basic 
intent of making regulations in line with contemporary global standards for 
clinical trials.  
The Government has brought out detailed guidelines on Good Clinical 
Practices (GCP), which are also required to be followed during conduct of a 
trial. These are also at par with very stringent international practices. 
The Ministry has conducted several training programs with the support of 
WHO to make clinical research stakeh olders aware of the new regulations 
and to impart them training on complying with the highest standards. 
While it has been made mandatory that Sponsors conduct periodic 
monitoring and audits of the studies, a process for conducing regulatory 
inspections has also been initiated. More than 30 subject experts from 
various medical institutions and Central Drugs Standard Control 
Organization, have undergone a training workshop which was held in  
coordination with Department of Pharmacology, All India Institute of 
Medical

Sciences, New Delhi, to equip them to carry out regulatory inspections of 
clinical trials.

Ban on smoking scenes in films and TV serials 
*145. SHRI LALIT SURI : Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have imposed a ban on smoking scenes in films 
and Television serials with effect from 2nd October, 2005; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) the reaction of film industry, if any, received by Government; and 
(d) how Government propose to tackle foreign films having smoking scenes 
released in theatres? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. 
ANBUMANI RAMADOSS): (a) to (d) Based on the WHO study that 76% of 
the Indian movies portrayed tobacco consumption and existence of a strong 
linkage between films and youth behaviour;the Cohort study published in the 
Lancet (2003) revealing that 52% of smoking initiation amongst children can be 
attributed to exposure to smoking in films; and the provisions contained in the 
"The Cigarettes and other Tobacco Products (Prohibition of Advertisement and 
Regulation of Trade and Commerce, Production, Supply and Distribution) Act, 
2003" prohibiting any person to promote the use or -consumption of tobacco 
products, the Government of India notified on 31.05.2005 "The Cigarettes and 
other Tobacco Products [Prohibition of Advertisement and Regulation of Trade 
and Commerce, Production, Supply and Distribution (Amendment)] Rules, 
2005" imposing a ban on display of to bacco products and their usage in 
movies/television. This is in addition to the existing provisions under the 
Cinematograph Act, 1952 read with rules framed thereunder to  the effect that 
scenes fending to encourag e, justify or glamorize consumption of tobacco or 
smoking are not shown. In a recent study  on "Exposure to movie smoking: Its 
relations to smoking initiation among US adolescents", published in 
PEDIATRICS, corroborates that smoking in movies is a risk factor for smoking 
initiation among US 
11 

RAJYA SABHA [2 December, 2005] 
adolescents. Limiting exposure of young adolescents to movie smoking could 
have important public health implications. 
Taking into consideration the technical  issues raised by the Ministry of 
Information & Broadcasting and the difficulties pointed out by the film 
industry, the Government has notified on 30th November 2005 to provide for 
certain relaxation/exemptions in the rules. As per these provisions no 
individual or a person or a character in cinema and television programmes 
shall display tocacco products or their use. Exemptions to these provisions 
are: 
• Indian films and televisions programmes displaying use of tobacco 
products necessary to represent the smoking or tobacco usage of a real 
historical figure or for representationof a historical era 
• Old Indian films and TV programmes produced prior to coming effect 
of this notification 
• foreign films and television programmes, including dubbed or sub-
titled foreign films or television programmes 
• Indian or foreign films and TV programmes clearly reflecting the 
dangers of tocacco use 
• live coverage of news, current affa irs, interviews, public meetings, 
sports events, cultural events being telecast on television 
These exemption are however subject to the conditions: 
• that it will not extend to display of  brands of tobacco product or 
product placement, close ups of tobacco products 
• it shall be mandatory for the film to  include anti-tobacco health spots 
at the beginning, middle and end of the said film 
• in case of television programmes, it shall be mandatory for placement 
of anti-tobacco health warnings as a prominent scroll at the bottom of 
the screen or airing of anti-tobacco health spots. 
These provisions will come into effect from 1st January 2006.

Scheduled

RAJYA SABHA [2 December, 2005] 
drugs and formulations based thereon are fixed by the National 
Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA)  in accordance with the provisions 
of para 7 of the Drugs (Prices Control) order, 1995 (DPCO, 95). A price of a 
Scheduled formulation is fixed by allowing Maximum Allowable Post 
Manufacturing Expenses (MAPE) @ 100% on ex-factory cost for 
indigenously manufactured Scheduled formulations and up to 50% of the 
landed cost for imported Scheduled formulations. The trade margin to 
retailers in respect of Scheduled formulations is fixed at 16%. 
Prices of non-Scheduled medicines are fixed by the manufacturers 
themselves keeping in view various factors like cost of production, 
marketing/selling expenses, R&D expenses, trade commission, market 
competition, product innovation, product quality etc. The Government takes 
corrective measures where the public interest is found to be adversely 
affected.

regularly monitors the movement of prices of medicines of mass consumption 
marketed through trade channel and intervenes whenever instances of 
unreasonable increase in prices affecting public interest adversely are noticed. 
The National Pharmaceutical Pricing Au thority (NPPA) has collected data 
on trade margin being offered by the manufacturers to the retailers for a 
limited sample. It was noted that some manufacturers had offered high margin 
to the retailers. However, the market share of such medicines was small. 
A Committee under the Chairmansh ip of Joint Secretary (PI) was 
constituted to examine the span of price control (including trade margin) in 
the light of National Common Minimum Programme and the observations of 
the Supreme Court in SLP No. (C) 3668/2003 and to suggest measures for 
fulfilling the objective of National Common Minimum Programme to ensure 
the availability of life saving drugs at reasonable prices. This Committee has 
submitted its interim report to the Government. The Committee has 
recommended, inter-alia, intensive monitoring on the prices of all those drugs 
out of the selected basket (National List of Essential Medicines, 2003) which 
are not under price control, ceilings on trade margins of drugs, a system of 
price negotiations for the new patented drugs, special schemes for people 
below poverty line, introduction of Rajasthan Model of Life Line Fluid Stores

patented drug, efforts to increase public awareness, wide publicity to policies 
and decisions of the Government and NPPA etc. Follow-up action on the 
recommendations made by the Committee in its interim report has been 
initiated. 
Subsequently, a Task Force under the Chairmanship of Dr. Pronab Sen, 
Principal Adviser, Planning Commission was constituted to explore options 
other than price control to make available life saving drugs at reasonable 
prices. During its meetings, the Task Fo rce deliberated upon almost all the 
recommendations made in its Interim Report by the Committee under the 
Chairmanship of Joint Secr etary. The Task Force has submitted its report to

(d) the details of the steps taken, so far, to honour the Supreme Court's 
directive and the commitment made in by Government? 
THE MINISTER OF CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS AND 
MINISTER OF STEEL (SHRI RAM VILAS PASWAN): (a) to (d) The 
Government announced the 'Pharmaceutic al Policy 2002' in February 2002. 
However, a public interest litigation filed in the High Court of Kanataka at 
Bangalore resulted in an Order dated 12-11-02, which stopped the 
government from implementing the price control regime of the 
Pharmaceutical Policy 2002. This Depart ment filed a Special Leave Petition 
(SLP) before the Supreme court of Indi a against the Order of the Karnataka 
High Court, which has been admitted as SLP (C) No. 3668/2003. The 
Supreme Court vide its order dated 10.3.2003 directed the government, inter-
alia, that, "we suspend the operation of the order to the extent it directs that 
the Policy dated 15.2.2002 shall not be implemented. However we direct that 
the petitioner shall consider and formulate appropriate criteria for ensuring 
essential and life saving drugs not to fall out of the price control and further 
directed to review drugs, which are e ssential and life saving in nature till 2nd 
May, 2003". Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has brought out the 
National List of Essential Medicines, 2003 after the review of the National 
Essential Drugs List, 1996. The matter is sub-judice before the Supreme 
Court. 
The National Common Minimum Programme as adopted by the 
government aims, inter-alia, to ensure availability of life saving drugs at 
reasonable prices. In the light of National Common Minimum Programme 
and the observations of the Supreme Court in SLP © No. 3668/2003, the 
Government constituted a Committee under the Chairmanship of Joint 
Secretary (PI) to suggest measures fo r fulfilling the objectives of National 
Common Minimum Programme to ensure the availability of life saving drugs 
at reasonable prices. This Committee has submitted its interim report to the 
government. The Committee has recommended, inter-alia, intensive 
monitoring on the prices of all those drugs out of the selected 
32 

[2 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
basket (National List of Essential Medicines, 2003) which are not under price 
control, ceilings on trade margins of drugs, a system of price negotiations for 
the new patented drugs, special schemes for people below poverty line, 
introduction of Rajasthan Model of Life Line Fluid Stores (hospital 
pharmacy stores run by Medicare Societies) for bulk purchase of drugs 
directly from manufacturer and selling them at reduced prices, compounding 
of offences under the Essential Comm odities Act, establishment of DPCO 
cells in all States on the model of Kamataka, price negotiations at the time of 
launching of new patented drug, effort s to increase public awareness, wide 
publicity to policies and decisions of the Government and NPPA etc. Follow-
up action on the recommendations made by the Committee in its interim 
report has been initiated. 
A Task Force under the Chairmanship  of Dr. Pronab Sen, Principal 
Adviser, Planning Commission was constituted to explore options other than 
price control to make available life saving drugs at reasonable prices. The 
Task Force has submitted its report to the Government on the 20th 
September, 2005. Some of the salient recommendations of Task Force are, 
the Price Controls should be imposed on the 'essentiality' of the drug and not 
on the basis of turnover and it should be applied only to formulations and not 
to bulk drugs. Some of the other major recommendations of Task Force are to 
promote generic drugs, to encourage public health facilities, to revive the 
Public Sector Enterprises in the manufacture of drugs, to provide fiscal 
incentives in R&D activities in drugs to provide financial support for 
implementation of Schedule M of Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, to enact Drugs 
and Therapeutics (Regulation) Act, to establish a National Authority on 
Drugs and Therapeutics (NADT), to establish price negotiation process for 
new patented drugs, to streamline the bulk procurement regime, to exempt 
the excise duty, customs duty and other levies on cancer and anti HIV/AIDS 
drugs, to establish the State Illness Funds in the States/Union Territories for 
BPL families, to reduce the excise duty on durgs from 16 to 8% to enhance 
the exemption limit of SSI units from Rs. 1 crore to Rs. 5 crores, to establish 
a Settlement Commission which is authorized to settle the disputed 
overcharged amount from the pharma companies. 
The Government in consultation with various stakeholders is examining 
the recommendations of the Task Force. Based on this a new Pharmaceutical 
Policy is likely to be announced shortly.

1050. DR. K. MALAISAMY: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be 
pleased to state:

per acre is much less of what can be achieved, if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(d) whether there will be an integrated approach to improve the yield and 
productivity? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTUR E (SHRI SHARAD PAWAR): (a) 
Agriculture provides livelihood to about 650 millions people. Of these, about 
79% belong to small and marginal farmer category. 
(b) The Government is cognizant of the needs of the farming community 
including small and marginal farmers. To improve their conditions, a number 
of measures have been taken. These include easy and timely availability 
41 

RAJYA SABHA [2 December, 2005] 
of institutional credit at low rate of interest, better risk management through 
crop insurance scheme, encourgement to contract farming, promotion of 
agricultural diversification towards income enhancing crops and activities 
suitable to small holdings, better market and storage facilities, sustainable 
dry-land farming, subsidy and price support measures like payment of 
Minimum Support Prices to prevent distress sales by the farmers. 
(c) and (d) With adoption of modern technologies, there has been many 
fold increase in the yield of several crops. The yield of wheat, for example, is 
comparable with the worl d average, which stood at 2742 kg/hectare as 
compared to world average at 2725 kg./hectare in 2001. Similarly, yield of 
sugarcane was much higher at 70617 kg/.hectare in 2001 than the world 
average of 65204 kg/. hectare. However, in other crops, much more needs to 
be done. A number of measures have been taken by the Government to rasie 
the yield in agricultural sector which include subsidies for modern inputs like 
seeds and fertilizers, integrated pest management, agricultural machinery, 
drip irrigation system and easy and timely availability of credit at low rate of 
interest to enable farmers to adopt modern technology for improving the 
resource use efficiency. The price and market support measures also 
constitute an important ingredient of the integrated approach to improve the 
yield and productivity of agriculture sector.

meeting their credit requirements and for provide relief to the 
indebted farmers, the Government has taken several measures and 
has advised the banks to:— 
(i) To increase the agricultural credit flow at the rate of 30% per year. 
(ii) To restructure the outstanding debt of the farmers under the following 
heads in accordance with the guidelines issued by Reserve bank of 
India (RBI) National Bank for Agriculture & Rural Development 
(NABARD); 
Farmers in distress—Rescheduling/restructuring of the outstanding 
loan of the farmers as on 31st Ma rch, 2004 in the districts declared 
as calamity-affected by the Stat e Government. Rescheduled loan 
shall be repayable over a period of five years, at current interest 
rates, including an initial moratorium of two years. 
47 

RAJYA SABHA [2 December, 2005] 
Farmers in arrears—Loans in default of farmers who have become 
ineligible for fresh credit as their earlier debts have been categorized 
as substandard or doubtful shall be rescheduled as per the guidelines 
so that such farmers become eligible for fresh credit. 
On restructuring as above, the farmers will become eligible for fresh 
loans. 
(iii) To grant a one-time settlement (OTS) including partial waiver of 
interest or loan to the small and marginal farmers who have been 
declared as defaulters and have be come ineligible for fresh credit. 
Banks have also been advised to review cases where credit has been 
denied on the sole ground that a loan account was settled through 
compromise or write offs. 
(iv) In some parts of the country, farmers face acute distress because of the 
heavy burden of debt from non-in stitutional lenders (e.g. private 
moneylenders). Banks have been permitted to advance loans to such 
farmers for redeeming their debt from private moneylender and for 
providing them relief from indebtedness. 
(v) All the public sector banks have been advised to reduce their lending 
rate for agriculture to a single digit rate of not more than 9% per 
annum on crop loans upto a Ceiling of Rs. 50,000/-. This rate will 
benefit most of the crop loan account holders and will cover almost all 
the small and marginal farmers.

50,000 and agri-business and agri-clinics up to Rs. 5 lakh.

1059. DR. GYAN PRAKASH PILANIA: Will the Minister of

land due to prolonged use of chemicals/inorganic fertilizers. However, 
investigation under All India Coordinated Research Project under Indian 
Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR) on "Long Term Fertilizer 
Experiments' over few decades have revealed that prolonged imbalanced use 
of chemical fertilizers and non application of organic manures affected soil 
health and crop productivity by causing deficiencies of secondary and micro 
nutrients. The average consumption of fertilizers in the country is 89.83

any ill effect on the fertility of the land. The ICAR is recommending soil test 
based Integrated Nutrient Management practices to avoid loss of fertility. 
Besides, Govt, is also promoting Integrated Nutrient Management (INM) 
which includes soil test based balanced and judicious use of chemical 
fertilizers in conjunction with organic fertilizers like Farm Yard Manure, 
green manure, compost, vermicompost and biofertilizers etc. for sustaining 
soil health and its productivity.

(c) whether it is also a fact that the soil erosion is to the extent of 400 
tonnes per hectare in the country every year; 
(d) if so, the facts in this regard and whether any action plan has been 
evolved at the national level by Government to check the soil erosion; and 
(e) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI SHARAD PAWAR): (a) 
and (b) The soil formation and erosion is a natural process occurring 
simultaneously to maintain the equilibrium in eco-system. Due to over 
exploitation, unscientific use of natural resources and other reasons, the land 
denudation is more than natural fo rmation. The study conducted by the 
Central Soil and Water Conservation Research and Training Institute— 
Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR), Regional Centre, Dehradun 
revealed that there is reduction in yi elds of the crops and income to the 
farmers due to loss of top soils. 
(c) to (e) As per available estimate, the average rate of soil erosion in the 
country is 16.4 tonnes per hectare per year. With a view to sustain 
agricultural productivity, control of soil erosion, water conservation and 
prevention of land degradation, Government of India, Ministry of Agriculture 
is implementing four Watershed Development Programmes/Schemes, 
namely, (i) National Watershed Development Project for Rainfed Area 
(NWDPRA); (ii) Soil Conservation fo r Enhancing the Productivity of 
Degraded Lands in the Catchments of River Valley Projects Flood Prone 
River (RVP & FPR); (iii) Reclamation of Alkali Soil (RAS); (iv) Watershed 
Development Project for Shifting Cultivation Area (WDPSCA) and few 
Externally Aided Projects (EAPs). Three Watershed Development 
Programmes, viz., (i) Drought Prone Area Programme (DPAP); (ii) Desert 
Development Programme (DDP) and (iii) Integrated Wasteland Development 
Project (IWDP) are being implemented by Ministry Rural Development. In 
addition to these, Ministry of Environment & Forest is implementing a 
National Afforestation & Eco-Development Project Scheme (NAEPS) for 
soil and water conservation and afforestation. Under these programmes, since 
inception upto March 2005, an area of 28,533 million ha. has been developed 
with expenditure of Rs. 14577.32 crore. The working Group on Watershed 
Development, Rainfed Farming and Natural Resource Management for Tenth 
Five Year Plan, constituted by Planning Commission has suggested a 
perspective plan for development of

88.5 million ha. area in 20 years through Watershed Development 
Programmes. Accordingly,  an area of 21.4 million ha. has been proposed 
for checking erosion, land degradation and thereby sustaining agricultural

estimated cost of Rs. 6422.95 crore during X Five Year Plan. An amount 
of Rs 1497.00 crore has been allocated for treatment of 3.36 million ha. area 
during 2005-06 under various watershed development programmes as per

Price increase of life saving drugs 
1077. SHRI TARIQ ANWAR: Will the Minister of CHEMICALS AND 
FERTILIZERS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the prices  of life saving drugs have to be 
increased in the near future; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that recommendations have been given for 
constitution of single regulator of prices of drugs; and 
(d) if so, what are its recommendations and the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS AND 
MINISTER OF STEEL (SHRI RAM VI LAS PASWAN): (a) to (d) The 
Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 1995 (DPCO, 95) does not make any 
distinction between Life Saving drugs and other drugs. There is no specific 
norms or guidelines to determine as to  which drugs can be classified as life 
saving drugs. Every drug, in general, is considered useful in saving and 
prolonging of life. 
As per the present Pharma Pricing Po licy, the 74 bulk drugs specified in 
the First Schedule of the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 1995 (DPCO, 95) and 
the formulations based thereon are under price control and their prices are 
fixed/revised by the National Pharmaceu tical Pricing Authority (NPPA) in 
accordance with the provisions of the DPCO, 95. 
Prices of non-Scheduled formulations are fixed by the manufacturers 
themselves keeping in view the various factors like cost of production, 
marketing/selling expenses, R&D expenses, trade commission, market 
competition, product innovation, product quality etc., The NPPA monitors 
the prices of medicines as per monthly Retail Audit Reports of ORG-IMS 
Research Pvt. Ltd. The Government takes corrective measures where the 
public interest is found to be adversely affected. 
Fixation/revision of prices of Scheduled formulations is an ongoing 
activity undertaken by the NPPA under the provisions of the DPCO, 1995. 
A Task Force under the Chairmanship of Dr. Pronab Sen, Principal 
Adviser, Planning Commission was constituted to explore options other than 
price control to make available life saving drugs at reasonable prices. The 
Task Force has submitted its report to the Government on the 20th 
September, 2005. The Task Force has recommended, inter-alia, for 
constitution of single regulator of prices of drugs. 
71 

RAJYA SABHA [2 December, 2005] 
The Government in consultation with various stakeholders is examining 
the recommendations of the Task Force.  Based on this a new Pharmaceutical 
Policy is likely to be announced shortly.

Statement 
Recommendations made by M/s Mc Kinsey and Co. in its report 
• Adopting a multi-tiered debt structure and reducing working capital 
borrowings. 
• Optimizing rail movement using a linear programme. 
• Consolidating handling and road transportation contracts within 
regions and outsourcing to large logistic service providers. 
• Purchasing consolidated requirement of gunny bags through open 
' tender and reimbursing farmers/millers/arthias for supplying paddy 
in used gunnies. 
• Procuring directly at RSI depots or rice mills in Punjab and Haryana 
• Renting excess capacity to third parties, i.e. private grain companies, 
logistic service providers. 
• Appointing 3rd party agency to monitor stock moved by rail and to 
check transit losses. 
• Reimbursing State agencies for st ocks carried by them prior to 
actual delivery to the FCI. 
• Revision of staffing norms and initiatives to increase staff 
productivity. 
• Revising incentive norms, balancing labour capacity and retiring 
excess labour. 
• Reducing obligatory expenses by ha ving the market intermediaries 
perform additional tasks in the mandis. 
• Reimbursement of procurement incide ntals to State agencies to the 
bench market to the cost incurred by the FCI; linking custody and 
maintenance charges to quality of storage infrastructure, and 
building year to year cost reduc tion/efficiency improvement clauses 
in the supplier contracts/MoU with State agencies.

1092. SHRI EKANATH K. THAKUR: Will the Minister of 
CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the much -hyped Targetted Public Distribution 
System (TPDS) for supplying subsidised foodgrain to Below Poverty Line 
(BPL) families has failed; 
93 

RAJYA SABHA [2 December, 2005] 
(b) whether as per the findings of Government's programme evaluation 
organization, the transition from universal PDS to TPDS has neither 
benefited the poor nor helped reduce budgetary food subsidies in the desired 
manner; 
(c) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(d) the steps Government propose to take to improve the system? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (DR. AKHILESH 
PRASAD SINGH): (a) No Sir. The main objective of the Targetted Public 
Distribution System (TPDS) is to en sure availability of foodgrains at 
reasonable prices to Below Poverty Line (BPL) families in the country. The 
increasing trend of offtak e of foodgrains under BPL indicate that TPDS is 
effective. The-implementation of TPDS  is the joint responsibility of the 
Central and the State Governments. While the Central Government is 
responsible for procurement, storage and transportation of foodgrains upto the 
nearest . Principal Distribution Cent res of FCI in each State/UTrthe 
identification of BPL families, issue of ration cards and issue of licences to the 
fair price shops and distribution of foodgrains to the beneficiaries is the 
responsibility of the respective State Governments/UTs. Government have 
occasionally received complaints in this respect and these have been 
forwarded to the concerned State Governments/UTs for appropriate action. 
(b) and (c) The study conducted  by the Programme Evaluation 
Organisation of the Planning Commission have taken the sample size of 240 
Fair Price Shops (FPS) and 3600 households in 60 districts of 18 selected 
States. Whereas the TPDS covers the entire population and there are more 
than 4.78 lakh FPSs spread all over the c ountry. As many as 120 mobile Fair 
Price Shops were selected for the stud y which may be less than 1 % of the 
total FPSs in the co untry. The study has not be en conducted in difficult 
terrains/areas like Andaman & Nicobar islands, Lakshadweep, J & K, 
Nagaland, Manipur etc., where the TPDS is more relevant. The Study also 
ignored the concentration of BPL benefici aries, in the selection of the study 
design units. As many as 25% of the total households selected were non-
oeneficiary households. The study have not indicated the confidence level 
and the sampling error. In view of this, it is not appropriate to draw the 
conclusion by the PEO study that the TPDS has not benefited the poor. 
(d) Reforms in TPDS to improve its efficiency, accountability and 
effectiveness is an ongoing process. Besides notification of the Public 
Distribution System (Control) Order, 2001, involvement of the Panchayati

Indian Fair Price Shops Dealers Fede ration, and a meeting with all the 
members of Parliament was organized for strengthening of TPDS Regional 
Conferences are also being held with focus on the unique problems of the

Control Boards (SPCBs) and Pollution Control Committees (PCCs) of Union

also to submit the inventory reports to the Central Pollution Control Board. 
The Government have notified the Hazardous Waste (Management & 
Handling) Amendment Rules, 2003 and also to submit the inventory reports 
to the Central Pollution Control Board. The Government have notified the 
Hazardous Waste (Managem ent & Handling) Rules, 1989 as amended, to 
regulate and properly manage the hazardous waste generated in the country as 
well as the wastes imported into the country for recycling purposes. Rule-5 of 
these Rules provides that every occupier  handling, or a recycler recycling 
hazardous waste shall obtain authorization from the respective State Pollution 
Control Boards or Pollu tion Control Committees fo r collection, reception,

HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the scientists in Indian Institute of Science 
(lISc), Bangalore, found a new method to fight brain cancer; 
(b) if so the details thereof; 
(c) which are the twenty genes that have been identified by the scientist at 
the lISc to fight brain cancer; 
(d) whether it is also a fact that the scientists are thinking of developing a 
DNA chip to predict the progression of brain cancer in a patient; and 
(e) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (c) The 
Director General, Indian Council of Me dical Research has informed that as 
per a recent publication from Indian Institute of Science, Bangalore, 
expression of several thousand genes in tissue samples of brain cancer were 
studied. The investigators have informed that using microarray expressions 
and other valid techniques they have identified 67 genes including 
obteonectin, vimentin, seemaphorin 4D, B2 microglobulin, HES, jagged 1 
etc. 
(d) and (e) Research for newer ways of treatment and remediation of 
cancer diseases including brain cancer is an ongoing process. Current level of 
research is insufficient to predict the possibility of developing a DNA chip 
for the purpose of predicting progression of brain cancer in a patient.

1127.   SHRI SANJAY RAUT: 
SHRI B.K. HARIPRASAD: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the recent UNDP's 
human development report on increasing high infant and maternal mortality 
rates in the country, particularly in Maharashtra State; 
121 

RAJYA SABHA [2 December, 2005] 
(b) whether Bangladesh has fared much better in tackling infant mortality 
and malnutrition problems than India; and 
(c) if so, the details of steps taken or proposed to be taken for reducing the 
growth rates of infant and maternal mortality and banish malnutrition among 
children in the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) and (b) 
The UNDP's Human Development Report-2005 mentions that the annual rate 
of decline in child mortality in India has decreased from 2.9% in 1980 to 
2.3% since 1990. The report also menti ons that the rate of decline in child 
mortality has been higher in Bangladesh than in India during this period. The 
UNDP report, however, does not examine the infant mortality rate. 
According to data on infant and child mortality rates in India available from 
the Sample Registration System of Registrar General of India, both infant 
mortality rate and child mortality rate have shown a consistent declining 
trend over the years. The same is also true for the State of Maharashtra where 
the infant mortality rate has shown a decline from 45 per thousand live births 
in 2001 to 42 per thousand live births in 2003. 
(c) Government of India have recently launched the National Rural Health 
Mission which aims at providing effectiv e health care including child health 
and safe motherhood services to rural population throughout the country with 
special focus on those states which have weak public health indicators. The 
mission seeks to improve access of serv ices especially to poor women and 
children for equitable, affordable, accou ntable and effective primary health 
care. The Reproductive and Child He alth Programme which aims at 
accelerating decline in infant, child and maternal mortality rates is an integral 
part of this mission. 
Under the Reproductive & Child Health Programme interventions for 
improving maternal and child health are being implemented in all districts of 
the country. The interventions for children include Immunization against six 
vaccine preventable diseases, control of  deaths due to diarrhoea and Acute 
Respriatory Infections, Prophylaxis for Vitamin A deficiency, Iron deficiency 
anemia and Essential Newborn Care. For the mothers the interventions 
include essential obstetric care; emer gency obstetric care; provision of 
referral transport through panchayats and provisions of drugs and equipments 
at first referral units.

Spread of 'Hanta Virus' 
1132. SHRI ABU ASIM AZMI: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Govenment are aware about th e surfacing of 'Hanta Virus' a 
deadly life threatening disease in the country; 
(b) if so, the number and details of such cases; 
(c) the details of the treatment of the patients; and 
(d) the steps being taken by Government to prevent its surfacing in the 
country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (d)As 
per the information recei ved from Indian Council of Medical Research, 
recent study conducted by the Christian Medical College (CMC), Vellore and 
published in Indian Journal of Medical Research is the first report of the 
presence of Hanta Virus infection in  humans in India. The 'Study for 
Serological evidence of Hanta virus in fection in human population in South 
India  was done on serum samples from 152 fever patients showing 
symptoms of dengue and leptospirosis. Out of these patients, 23 were found 
positive for Anti-Hanta virus IgM. Inaddition, 87 blood donors were also 
studied in which 5.7% were found to be positive for Anti-Hanta virus IgM. 
These findings indicate the possibility of the presence of Hantavirus infection 
in India. 
There is no specific treatment for Hant a virus infection, only symptomatic 
and supportive therapy is provided. However, Ribavinn is found to be 
effective in complicated infections of Hanta virus.

qualification for enrollment as medical practitioner in the country in which 
the institution awarding the said qualif ication is situated and which is 
equivalent to MBBS in India. 'The Eligibility Requirement for taking 
admission in an undergraduate medical course in a Foreign Medical 
Institution Regulations, 2002' prescribes that a person who is a citizen of 
India shall not on or after 15.3.2002 be eligible to get admission to obtain 
medical qualification in a medical ins titution in any foreign country without

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) and (b) 
According to National Family Health Survey (NFHS)-II of 1998,51.8% of 
ever married 
133 

RAJYA SABHA [2 December, 2005] 
women (15-49 years) were found to have anemia. 35% had mild anemia; 
14.8% moderate anemia and only 1.9% severe anemia. Among the anemic 
children percentage with anemia are 74.3% in the age group 6 to 35 months. 
Out of this, 22.9% had mild anemia; 45.9% moderate anemia and 5.4% 
severe anemia. 
The major causes of nutritional anemia are  inadequate nutrition with 
deficient intake of iron and folic acid in diet, inadequate absorption of iron, 
frequent preganancies, high prevalence of infections and infestations and 
faulty feeding practices. 
Government of India has recently launched the National Rural Health 
Mission (NRHM) in order to improve the availability of and access to quality 
health care. The interventions under NRHM include RCH - II, Programme 
wherein Iron and Folic Acid tablets are provided to all anemic women who 
come for ante-natal check-up. The other important inteventions under NRHM 
include Janani Suraksha Yojana wherein cash incentives are provided for 
delivering a child at the health institution. Eight EAG States, J&K and Assam 
have been provided with a scheme of village link worker (ASHA). ASHA 
will orient the community on the importance of nutrition and shall be 
provider for IFA tablets besides orienting the community on the other health 
related issues. 
Iron deficiency is a problem of inadequate nutrition. A national 
Nutritional Policy was formulated in 1993 and the national plan of action on 
nutrition is being implemented through a number of Departments of 
Government of India including, among other, the Integrated Child 
Development Services Programme of Department of Women and Child 
Development and the Reproductive and Child Health Programme of the 
Department of Family Welfare for improving the nutritional status of 
pregnant women and children. 
Apart from health related factors illiteracy, poverty, general economic and 
social development has a direct bear ing on the incidence of anemia among 
people, particularly among women. To tackle these problems, various 
departments of the Government are also implementing programmes such as 
Nutrition education of the community in rural, urban and tribal areas by the 
Food and Nutrition education of the community in rural, urban and tribal 
areas by the Food and Nutrition Board of the Department of Women and 
Child Development with a view to create awareness about the consequences 
of anemia, promote the locally available foods rich in iron and on folic acid 
and how to prevent and control anaemia.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) The 
World Health Organisation's publicati on "Inheriting the World: Atlas of 
children and the Health Environment"  examines the effects of various

countries according to mortality rates.  According to this classification,

environmental sanitation are important contributors to child mortality due to 
diarrhoeal diseases. In addition, air pollution is one of the important causes 
of acute respiratory infections among children which is another major cause 
of child mortality. 
Safe Drinking Water and improvement in sanitation services are 
recognized as important interventions in preventing diarrhea. Govt, of India 
is implementing the Central Rural Sanitation Programme. Under this, the 
Department of Drinking Water Supply is implementing Total Sanitation 
Campaign (TSC). Govt, of India has sanctioned Total Sanitation Campaign 
(TSC) projects in 520 districts of the country to improve the sanitation 
scenario in the villages. The objectiv es of the TSC Programme are to bring 
about an improvement in the general quality of life in the rural areas, 
accelerate sanitation coverage, generate  felt demand for sanitation facilities 
through awareness creation and Health Education. Further the National Rural 
Health Mission (NRHM) recently launched by the Govt, of India seeks to 
converge health concerns with determinants of health, sanitation, hygiene, 
nutrition and safe drinking water.

deficiency under the RCH Programme of National Rural Health Mission and 
supply of iodated salt in place of  common salt under National Iodine

control of Micronutrient Deficiencies per se in five States is also in

Bird Flu 
1153. SHRI TARIQ ANWAR: 
SHRI ANAND SHARMA: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY W ELFARE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that there is a threat of bird flu in the country; 
(b) what steps have been taken to face this disease; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that India does not have sufficient stocks of 
influenza vaccines; and 
(d) the steps proposed for the production and availability of Avian Flu 
Vaccine in the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (d) 
World Health Organization (WHO) has issued an alert that Bird Flu could 
spread to India and other countries from the very first time that the current 
outbreak of Avian Influenza Virus (H5N1) was first detected in the republic 
of Korea in December, 2003. 
No case of Bird Flu (Avian Influenza) has been reported in India either in 
humans or birds. 
However, Government of India took adequate measures to prevent entry 
of Avian Influenza in to India and to contain the disease if it has to happen in 
poultry or humans. The measures instituted are: 
• A joint Monitoring Group under the Chairemanship of Director 
General of Health Services consisting members from Indian Council 
of Medical Research, National Institute of Communicable Diseases, 
World Health Organization and Department of Animal Husbandry 
is monitoring the situation ever since the WHO alerted the global 
community and advising appropriate actions to the Government. 
• The Department of Animal Husbandry, Dairying & Fisheries has 
prepared and circulated an Action Plan for State Animal Husbandry 
Departments in respect of Bird Flu for taking action in case of 
suspicion of outbreak of the disease and also in the event of 
outbreak of Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI). 
Aconference of the State Secretaries of Animal Husbandry was held 
regarding preparedness in case of outbreak of the disease. 
153 

RAJYA SABHA [2 December, 2005] 
• Department of Animal Husbandry has intensified surveillance and 
disease intelligence. Samples so far tested at High Security Animal 
Disease Laboratory (HSADL), Bhopal were found negative. 
Training has been imparted to the staff of the State Wildlife and the 
Animal Husbandry Department, how to collect and dispatch the 
samples to the laboratory for testing. 
• There is a total ban in place agai nst import of poultry and poultry 
related products from all countries affected with bird flu outbreak. 
Even birds [grand parent stock of poultry etc.] imported from highly 
pathogenic avian influenza free countries are subjected to quarantine 
and screening. 
• Department of Environment and Forests has issued instructions to all 
their Wild Life Wardens to keep a watch on death of migratory birds 
in identified water bodies. Any unusual death among migratory birds 
would immediately be brought to the notice of Dept. of Animal 
Husbandry. 
• Ministry of Health and Family Welfare is regularly reviewing the 
situation. A National Consultation Meeting on Pandemic 
Preparedness was held on 1st August, 2005 with all stakeholders to 
finalize pandemic preparedness and Response Plan. 
• A contingency plan for managing human cases of avian influenza 
has been finalized detailing immediate action to be taken to deal 
with any suspected outbreak. The state level action plan has been 
discusses with the State Govts. 
• The components of the action plan such as hospital strengthening, 
Influenza Surveillance Network, Laboratory strengthening in terms 
of bio-safety labs, personal protective equipments, stockpiling of 
drugs and Information Education Communication are being taken up 
in a phased manner. 
• An inter Ministerial Task force has been constituted under the 
Chairmanship of Secretary (H&FW) to ensure availability of drugs, 
vaccines and all other aspects for ma nagement of avian influenza in 
the country. 
• National Institute of Communicable Diseases has been identified as 
the nodal agency for monitoring avian influenza and for 
investigating outbreaks. Under the aegis of ICMR, an Human 
Influenza surveillance network has been operationalized. 
154 

[2 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
•   The situation has also been reviewed by Committee of Secretaries on 
a monthly basis and Ministry of Home Affairs. 
There is no vaccine for Avian Flu [H 5N1] either for humans or birds. 
Seasonal influenza vaccine is available but it has no role in either preventing 
human cases of avian influenza [H5N1] or the pandemic strain which may 
evolve in future.

In addition, the Indian Medical Counc il (Professional Conduct, Etiquette 
& Ethics) Regulations, 2002, complaints with regard to professional 
misconduct can be brought before the Medical Council of India or the

action. If found guilty, appropriat e Medical Council may award such 
punishment as deemed necessary or may direct the removal altogether or for 
a specified period the name of the delinquent from the register of registered 
medical practitioners. 
The National Health Policy, 2002 en visages the participation of the

Court of India in the case of T.M.A. Pai Foundation & Others, v/s State of

fee structure and they are expected not to charge cap itation fee or indulge in

private medical institutes have the freedom to fix their own fee structure. 
However, each State Government is required to set up a Committee under the 
Chairmanship of a retired High Cour t Judge to decide whether the fee

Junk food habit among the people 
1164. SHRI VARINDEB SINGH BAJWA:  
          SHRI DARA SINGH: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether government are aware that junk food is fast gaining popularity 
in metropolitan cities like Mumbai, Chandigarh and Delhi wherein people 
are getting quickly attracted towardsit; 
(b) if so, whether the food experts the world over, have expressed their 
concern over increasing consumption of junk food as a large number of 
children and youth far failing victims; 
(c) if so, whether Government propose to take concrete steps to check the 
expanding junk food culture in order to save our children from its adverse 
impact; 
167 

RAJYA SABHA [2 December, 2005] 
(d) if so, by when; and 
(e) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (e) 
There is no specific definition for junk food. The phrase 'Junk food' is used to 
denote such food which have high level of calories and have little enzyme 
producing vitamins and minerals. When such food is consumed, the body is 
required to produce its own enzymes to convert these empty calories into 
usable energy. This is not desireable as this enzymes producing function in 
human body should be reserved for the performance of vital metabolic 
reactions. 
There is an increasing trend particularly among school children and 
adolescent population to consume 'Junk fo od' which is rich in calories but 
low in nutritive value. However, there is no large scale data on the extent of 
consumption of junk foods.  . 
There is a concerned world over regarding consumption of highly 
refined foods with only energy and little or no vitamins and minerals. 
There are studies to indicate that  there is a positive correlation 
between consumption of foods with empty calories and chronic degenerative 
diseases as well as hypertension, ob esity, cardio vascular problems and 
glucose intolerance. A study conducted by All India Institute of Medical 
Sciences (AIIMS) - Department of Science & Technology (DST) in 2002 
found that the consumption of junk food is increasing in schools and 
adolescent population. The same study has shown that this trend and 
associated life style factors in urban adolescent and young adult population 
has resulted in increase of non-co mmunicable disease among the young 
population. 
The need for education of general public to avoid junk food has 
increased and efforts are being made by Government, nutritionsts and 
dieticians to make people aware of its harmful effects. The Ministry of 
Health and Family Welfare has also  prepared IEC material advising 
avoidance of junk food by all age groups of the population. These materials 
have been circulated to all the States  and are also displayed and distributed 
during 'health melas' organized by this Ministry. The National Institute of 
Nutrition (NIN) has developed dietary guidelines for Indians, where it has 
been suggested that ready to eat should be consumed judiciously and "free 
sugar" should be used sparingly.

WHO report on flu pandemic 
1166. DR. M.A.M. RAMASWAMY: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the World Health Organisation has warned an outbreak of flu 
pandemic which may cause heavy damage to human lives; 
(b) if so, when the last time flu  pandemic attacked the number of human 
lives lost; 
171 

RAJYA SABHA [2 December, 2005] 
(c) the steps taken by Government to combat the outbreak of all kinds of 
flu, be it avain flu or human flu; and 
(d) the names of pharmaceutical companies which have started working on 
drugs to fight avain flu or human flu? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (d) 
World Health Organisation (WHO) has is sued an alert that Bird Flu could 
spread to India and other countries from  the very first time that the current 
outbreak of Avian Influenza Virus (H5N1) was first detected in the Republic 
of Korea in December, 2003. 
The H5N1 virus may undergo a genetic change, either mixing with 
existing human influenza strain or mutating of its own, giving rise to a 
pandemic strain to which human population has no immunity, giving rise to a 
pandemic. 
An estimated 40-50 million deaths occurred in the influenza pandemic of 
1918-1919. The pandemics of 1957 and 1968 respectively were caused by 
the milder virus, each killed 1 to 4 million people. 
No case of Bird Flu (Avian influenza) has been reported in India either in 
humans or birds in the current outbreak. 
However, Government of India took adequate measures to prevent entry 
of Avian Influenza in to India and to contain the disease if it has to happen in 
poultry or humans. The measures instituted are: 
* A Joint Monitoring Group under the Chairmanship of Director 
General 
of Health Services consisting members from Indian Council of Medical 
Research, National Institute of Communicable Diseases, World Health 
Organization and Department of Animal Husbandry is monitoring the 
situation ever since the WHO alerted the global community and advising 
appropriate actions to the Government. 
* The Department of Animal Husbandry, Dairying & Fisheries has 
prepared and circulated an Action Plan for State Animal Husbandry 
Departments in respect of Bird Flu for taking action in case of suspicion of 
outbreak of the disease and also in the event of outbreak of Highly 
Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI). A co nference of the State Secretaries of 
Animal Husbandry was held regarding preparedness in case of outbreak of 
the disease. 
* Department of Animal Husbandry has intensified surveillance and 
disease intelligence Samples so far tested at High Security Animal Disease 
172 

[2 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Laboratory (HSADL), Bhopal were found negative. Training has been 
imparted to the staff of the Stat e Wildlife and the Animal Husbandry 
Department, how to collect and dispatch the samples to the laboratory for 
testing. 
* There is a total ban in place against import of poultry and poultry related 
products from all countries affected with bird flu outbreak. Even birds [grand 
parent stock of poultry etc.] imported from highly pathogenic avian influenza 
free countries are subjected to quarantine and screening. 
* Department of Environment and Forests has issued instructions to all 
their Wild Life Wardens to keep a watch on death of migratory birds in 
identified water bodies. Any unusual death among migratory birds would 
immediately be brought to the notice of Dept. of Animal Husbandry. 
* Ministry of Health and Family Welfare is regularly reviewing the 
situation. A National Consultation Meeting on Pandemic Preparedness was 
held on 1st August, 2005 with all stakeholders to finalize pandemic 
preparedness and Response Plan. 
*A contingency plan for managing human cases of avian influenza has 
been finalized detailing immediate action to be taken to deal with any 
suspected outbreak. The state level actio n plan has been discussed with the 
State Govt. personal protective eq uipments, stockpiling of drugs and 
Information Education Communication are being taken up in a phased 
manner. 
* An Inter Ministerial Task Force has been constituted under the 
Chairmanship of Secretary (H&FW) to ensure availability of drugs, vaccines 
and all other aspects for management of Avian influenza in the country. 
* National Institute of Communicable Diseases has been identified as the 
nodal agency for monitoring Avian Influenza and for investigating outbreaks. 
Under the aegis of ICMR, and Human Influenza surveillance network has 
been operationalized. 
* The situation has also been reviewed  by Committee of Secretaries on a 
monthly basis and Ministry of Home Affairs. 
* There is no definitive treatment for human cases of avian influenza of a 
pandemic caused by a pandemic influe nza strain. Antiviral  drugs such as 
Oseltamivir, Zanamivir, Amantidine and Remantidine reduces viral load and 
improves the clinical outcome if given early. It is not known which drug 
would be effective for a pandemic stra in. For treatment of human cases of 
Avian Influenza Oseltamirvir is recommended.-M/s Roche of Switzerland

already manufactures the drug Osejtamivir (Tamiflu). Indian companies who 
have started working on the drug are M/s Cipla, M/s Hetero Drugs and M/s

Preventive mechanism for exploitation of the poor for clinical trials 
1168. SHRIMATI BRINDA KARAT : Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) what regulatory mechanism Government have set up to prevent the 
exploitation of poor people who voluntarily go for clinical trials; 
(b) in the context of many of the volunteers being uneducated persons, 
what are the guarantees that principle of informed consent is being followed; 
and 
(c) in view of the dangers, whether Go vernment are thinking of canceling 
the January, 2005 amendment to Schedule "Y" of the Drugs and Cosmetics 
Act? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN TH E MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (c) 
Detailed norms for conducting clinical trials on a new drug in the country are 
prescribed under Drugs & Cosmetics Rules 122-DA-122-E and also under 
Schedule Y to these rules. The clinical trial shall be initiated only after the 
permission from DCG(I) and approval from respective Ethics Committee is 
obtained. 
Schedule-Y prescribes the requirements for permission to conduct clinical 
trials and/or manufacture or import of New Drugs for marketing in India. It 
also lays down safety and ethical as pects, responsibilities of sponsors, 
investigators and Institutional Ethics Committee etc. Modalities for 
obtaining informed consent from trial subjects, and a specific form for the 
same have also been prescribed. During and following a subject's 
Participation in a trial, th e investigator has to ensure that adequate medical 
care is provided to participant for any adverse event. 
The Government has brought out detailed guidelines on Good Clinical 
Practices and Indian Council of Me dical Research (ICMR) had published 
Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical Re search on Human Subjects, which are 
required to be followed during conduct of a trial. 
These norms prescribed in India, are at par with international practices 
including that of U.S.A. Thus at present there is no requirement for canceling 
of the January 2005 amendment to Schedule-Y of Drugs & Cosmetics Act.

1174. SHRI B.J. PANDA: 
MS. PRAMILA BOHIDAR: 
. Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be pleased to state: . 
(a) whether it is a fact that the East Coast Railway has imposed a ban on 
booking of parcels weighing more than 20 kgs.; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that no other Zonal Railway has imposed such 
a ban; 
(c) if so, the rationale behind imposing this ban by the East Coast Railway; 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
180 

[2 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(d) whether this ban apart from hard-hitting the businessmen, 
agriculturalists and small scale industries in the State, is also resulting in the 
fall of parcel traffic income of the Zonal Railway; and 
(e) if so, the action plan of Government to address this issue? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS 
(SHRI R. VELU): (a) No general ban has been imposed on booking of parcel 
consignments weighing more than 20 kgs. Parcels of any quantity can be 
booked by rail subject to availability  of accommodation in train. However, 
any package weighing more than 20 kgs. are not accepted for booking as 
parcel traffic by any train, when it is clubbed and packed together w.e.f. 
1.7.2005. Perishable parcel traffic and single item package weighing more 
than 20 kgs. were exempted from this order. 
(b) and (c) Yes, Sir. With a view to streamline loading, East Coast 
Railway has imposed ban to avoid booking of heavy consignments. The 
main reasons for rationalisation are as under:—  
Merchants generally club many items to make a big package. Such a big 
and heavy package need three/ four persons to handle a single package. When 
number of heavy packages are many, train suffers detention for 
loading/unloading. 
Causes haphazard loading within th e Brakevan. Shelf space of the 
Brakevan remains unutilized. 
Causes jamming of passage and Brakevan door. 
Makes the packages dumped below or behind heavy packages untraceable 
at the enroute unloading points. 
Causes over carriage of parcels. 
Causes damage due to rough handling and delays in transit. 
The handling of too many heavy packages causes stress to the labourers. 
In view of the above, East Coast Railway has decided to reduce the weight 
of packages offered for booking as parcel traffic. The reduction in the number 
of heavy packages would make geographical stacking, utilization of shelf 
space, easier loading/unloading possibility  which would benefit the business 
and the railways. More parcels will reach their destination in time with less 
chances of damage. 
(d) The difficulties faced by merchants,  were taken into consideration in a 
review meeting taken by East Coast Railway and the limit of parcels has been 
increased from-20 kgs. to 30 kgs. w.e.f. 5.08.2005. This has been 
181

undertaken as an experiment on parcel  traffic by East Coast Railway and it 
has, been observed that the earnings on  parcel traffic from  the month of July 
2005 to October 2005 have increased by 5.21 % in comparison to the 
corresponding months of last year. 
(e) The subject will be reviewed in the normal course after gaining 
sufficient experience.

Vigilant Monitoring System during heavy rains 
1177. SHRI NANDI YELL AIAH: Will the Minister  of RAILWAYS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether in the midst of heavy rains and over-flooding of rivulets near 
culverts and railway bridges, there is any vigilant monitoring system through 
co-ordination of railway engineers and the concerned State's mandal-wise 
engineers and revenue authorities, to fore -see the dangers of railway track in 
advance; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor; and 
(d) the details of various measures alr eady in force to send messages to 
the engine driver to stop or slow down, when there is a danger to the railway 
track during the normal times and during the period of heavy rains? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS 
(SHRI R. VELU): (a) to (d) There are certain works carried out in the states 
like Irrigation Tanks and Water Reservoirs, Canals in embankments 
Marginal Bunds etc. which affect the safety of railway tracks and bridges. 
Such works are called 'Railway Affec ting Works'. It wa s therefore found 
necessary that Railway authorities are kept informed of the broad details and 
maintenance and upkeep of these works by the authorities concerned so that 
steps to ensure safety of track etc., if  necessary, could be taken in time. The 
attention of the Chief Ministers of States was drawn to the above during 
conference of chief Ministers with the Railway Minister in 5th June, 1957. It 
was decided to have State Committee of Engineers in each State consisting 
of officials from the Public Works Deptt., Irrigation, Revenue, Forest etc. of 
the States concerned and the Railway s. The State Committee of Engineers 
identify the Railway Affecting Works in  the State and also address various 
coordination issues. Government also had appointed a Committee of 
Engineers in 1967 under the Chairmanship of Dr. A.N. Khosla to study the 
various aspects related to the safety of Railway tracks and bridges with 
respect to floods. As a follow up of the recommendations of the Khosla 
Committee, accepted by the government, rules and procedures to be followed 
for the construction, maintenance, inspection and operation of 'Railway 
Affecting Works have bee laid down in the Manual of Instructions 
183 

RAJYA SABHA [2 December, 2005] 
for Railway Affecting Works to be uniformally adopted all over the country. 
This manual of instruction has been circulated to all State Goverments for 
approval and adoption. 
As per the laid down procedures, the parties owning the 'Railway 
Affecting Works' should regularly inspect and maintain these works as per 
the approved procedures and schedule laid down in the manual. Any repair or 
strengthening has to be carried out by them with utmost expedition before the 
onset of monsoon. Any request from Railway administration in connection 
with strengthening, repairs and maintenance and operation of all such works 
to esure safety of Railway lines is to be attended with promptitude. As per 
the laid down procedure, in case of any apprehended danger, or actual 
damage to a 'Railway Affecting work' which might affect the safety of 
Railway lines, immediate action has to be taken by the party concerned to 
advise the Station Master and the Railway Engineer concerned so as to 
enable the Railway officials to take  immediate precautionary measures to 
ensure safety of trains. The Railway engineer and the authorities owning the 
railway Affecting works also have to arrange with local authorities/village 
head men in whose jurisdiction 'Railway Affecting Works' are situated to 
watch them during periods of heavy rains and give timely intimation to 
nearest Station Master, if there is lik elihood of their failure. The Railway 
engineer in charge of the section also declares any section, which is likely to 
be affected by non-compliance of the urgently required repairs etc, as 
vulnerable and makes suitable arrangements for posting of Patrol 
men/Watchmen at the desired locations during heavy rains. These 
watchman/patrol men keep a watch at the vulnerable location and are 
equipped with signals to be displayed to  the driver/guard of  the train as well 
as detonators to be put on track for stopping or slowing the trains as required.

Statement 
The salient features of the National Steel Policy 
• The NSP sets out a broad roadmap for the Indian Steel Industry in its 
journey towards reform, restructuring and globalisation. 
• The long-term goal of the NSP is that India should have a modern 
and efficient steel industry of world standards, catering to diversified 
steel demand. The focus of the policy is to achieve global 
competitiveness not only in terms of cost, quality and product-mix 
but also in terms of global benechmarks of efficiency and 
productivity. 
• In order to achieve the goal of 110 million tonnes of steel production 
by 2019-20, the NSP seeks to remove the supply-side constraints to 
the growth of this industry in an open, globally integrated and 
competive environment. 
• The NSP seeks to adopt a multi-pronged strategy to move towards 
the long-term policy goal. On the demand side, the strategy would be 
to create incremental demand through  promotional efforts, creation 
of awarencess and strengthening the delivery chain, particularly in 
rural areas. On the supply side, the strategy would be to facilitate 
creation of aditional capacity, remove procedural and policy 
bottlenecks in the availability of inputs such as iron ore and coal, 
make higher investments in R&D and encourage the creation of 
infrastructure such as roads, railways, and ports. 
• The NSP acknowledges the low per capita consumption of steel in 
the country, especially in the rura l areas and the need to boost steel 
consumption to improve quality of life and help in meeting the 
growing aspirations of masses. 
• In order to achieve the strategic goal of 110 mT of steel production 
by 20 19-20, the industry would need addtional capital. In addtion, 
funds would be required for technological upgrade of existing 
facilities. In order to mobilize such vast resources NSP seeks to 
encourage foreign direct investment. In addition the policy also 
seeks to make the fiscal incentives, available to infrastructure 
projects, accessible to the steel industry. 
197 

RAJYA SABHA [2 December, 2005] 
• The NSP seeks to support developi ng of risk-hedging instruments 
like futures and derivatives to contain price volatility in the steel 
market. 
• The NSP seeks to strengthen the existing training and research 
facilities available to the domestic steel industry so as to provide 
suitable training programmes especially for the secondary small-
scale units and also to collect and analyze data on important 
parameters of the industry. 
• The NSP seeks to mount aggressive R&D efforts to create 
manufacturing capability for special types of steel, substitute coking 
coal, use iron ore fines, develop new products suited to rural needs, 
enhance material and energy efficiency, utilize waste, and arrest 
environmental degradation. 
• The NSP acknowleges the important role played by the secondary 
steel sector in providing employment, meeting local demand of steel 
in rural and semi-urban areas, and meeting the country's demand of 
some special products and seeks to endeavour to provide the 
necessary feedstock to these units at reasonable prices from major 
plants through the ex isting mechanism of State Small Industries 
Corporations. 
• The NSP recognizes the fact that intergration of the Indian steel 
industry with the global economy requires that the industry should 
be protected from unfair trade practices, which become common 
especially during periods of downturn. The NS P therefore, 
envisages, institution of mechanisms for import surveillance, and 
monitoring export subsidies in other countries.
